description: Memory consistency models and barriers decomposed. The contract between hardware and software about what orderings between memory accesses are visible to other cores. x86's TSO (strong); ARM/RISC-V/POWER's weak ordering. Acquire/release semantics. Memory barriers (fences) of various kinds. The relationship between hardware reorderings, compiler reorderings, and software-visible behaviour. C++/Rust/Java atomic ordering choices.

sub_mechanisms.name: sequential_consistency_definition
sub_mechanisms.definition: SC: there exists a single global ordering of all memory operations consistent with each program's program order; all cores see this same ordering.
sub_mechanisms.why: Easiest model to reason about for programmers. But hardware can't deliver SC efficiently — store buffers, write combining, out-of-order execution all break it. Most languages provide SC-DRF (data-race-free programs get SC behaviour).

sub_mechanisms.name: tso_total_store_order
sub_mechanisms.definition: x86's model. Sequential consistency EXCEPT loads may complete before earlier stores to different addresses. Store-load reordering allowed.
sub_mechanisms.why: x86 has a store buffer that holds stores until they retire. A subsequent load to a different address can pass the buffered store. To force ordering, MFENCE drains the store buffer.

sub_mechanisms.name: weak_ordering_arm_riscv
sub_mechanisms.definition: ARM/RISC-V/POWER: any load/store can be reordered with any other (between different addresses), unless explicit ordering is specified via barriers or release/acquire semantics.
sub_mechanisms.why: Maximum hardware flexibility = highest performance. Hardware can reorder freely; software must specify ordering explicitly where needed. Bugs from missing barriers are very common when porting from x86.

sub_mechanisms.name: store_buffer
sub_mechanisms.definition: Per-core buffer holding completed stores until they retire to L1 (and then potentially cache via coherence). Allows the core to continue executing past stores.
sub_mechanisms.why: Store buffer is why x86 isn't SC. The core sees its own stores (forwards from buffer to subsequent loads); other cores see stores only after retire to L1. This asymmetry creates the store-load reordering.

sub_mechanisms.name: store_forwarding
sub_mechanisms.definition: If a load matches a store still in the store buffer, the load gets the buffered value directly without going to cache.
sub_mechanisms.why: Common pattern: store X; load X. Without forwarding, the load would stall until the store completes. With forwarding, ~1 cycle. Critical for stack-heavy code (push then pop), recursive function returns.

sub_mechanisms.name: memory_barrier_full
sub_mechanisms.definition: x86 MFENCE / ARM DMB SY: orders ALL prior memory operations before ALL subsequent ones. Most expensive barrier.
sub_mechanisms.why: Strict ordering when needed. MFENCE drains the store buffer and waits for it to flush. DMB SY on ARM serialises everything. Used in lock primitives, init-then-publish sequences, IPC.

sub_mechanisms.name: memory_barrier_load
sub_mechanisms.definition: ARM DMB LD: ordering on prior loads only (subsequent loads + stores see them complete). Cheaper than DMB SY.
sub_mechanisms.why: Common case: 'check flag, then read data'. The flag check (load) must complete before data reads. DMB LD is sufficient and faster.

sub_mechanisms.name: memory_barrier_store
sub_mechanisms.definition: ARM DMB ST: ordering on prior stores only.
sub_mechanisms.why: Common case: 'write data, then set flag'. Data stores must be visible before flag store. DMB ST forces this ordering. Used in producer-consumer publishing.

sub_mechanisms.name: acquire_semantics
sub_mechanisms.definition: On a load: prevents subsequent memory operations from reordering before it. The classic 'acquire a lock' barrier.
sub_mechanisms.why: After acquiring a lock, subsequent reads/writes must stay after the lock acquire. Otherwise the protected critical section could leak. C++ memory_order_acquire, Rust Ordering::Acquire, Java volatile read all implement this.

sub_mechanisms.name: release_semantics
sub_mechanisms.definition: On a store: prevents prior memory operations from reordering after it. The classic 'release a lock' barrier.
sub_mechanisms.why: Before releasing the lock, all writes to the protected data must be visible. Otherwise another thread could acquire the lock and see partial writes. C++ memory_order_release, Rust Ordering::Release, Java volatile write all implement this.

sub_mechanisms.name: acquire_release_idiom
sub_mechanisms.definition: Pair of acquire + release on the same atomic variable forms a happens-before relationship: stores before the release are visible after the acquire.
sub_mechanisms.why: The fundamental synchronisation primitive. Build mutexes, condition variables, lock-free queues from acquire+release pairs. Captures the essential ordering without forcing full sequential consistency.

sub_mechanisms.name: relaxed_atomic
sub_mechanisms.definition: Atomic operation with no ordering guarantees: only atomicity of the access itself. C++ memory_order_relaxed, Rust Ordering::Relaxed.
sub_mechanisms.why: Cheapest atomic. Used for counters (where the count's exact ordering doesn't matter, only that increments don't lose updates). Hardware: typically just an atomic instruction without surrounding barriers.

sub_mechanisms.name: compiler_reordering
sub_mechanisms.definition: The compiler may reorder source-level memory accesses (within a single thread) as long as single-threaded semantics are preserved.
sub_mechanisms.why: Compiler optimisation. Stores to different addresses freely reorderable. Multi-thread correctness requires the programmer to use atomic/volatile/barriers — otherwise the compiler can move accesses freely. C++ memory model formalises what's allowed.

derivation_rules.name: weak_models_require_explicit_acquire_release
then: correct shared-memory code requires acquire/release pairs
derivation_rules.why: Without explicit barriers, hardware reorders freely. Producer-consumer code depends on data being visible before flag — without release-on-write + acquire-on-read, the flag may be visible before the data. C++/Rust/Java atomics provide the abstraction.

derivation_rules.name: store_buffer_creates_store_load_reordering
if: a CPU has a store buffer
then: loads can complete before earlier stores to different addresses
derivation_rules.why: Store buffer holds stores; loads pass them. To other cores, the load happened first. This is fundamental to x86's TSO model — the store buffer IS the source of the relaxation. Forcing strict order requires MFENCE (drain).

derivation_rules.name: acquire_release_pair_creates_happens_before
if: thread A does release-store on flag; thread B does acquire-load on flag
then: A's writes before release are visible to B after acquire
derivation_rules.why: The acquire/release pair establishes a synchronisation point. Hardware barriers + compiler barriers ensure the ordering. C++'s memory model formalises this; Java/Rust/C# all adopt the same semantics. Foundation of all lock-free synchronisation.

derivation_rules.name: barriers_must_appear_in_both_languages
then: both compiler barriers AND hardware barriers must be present
derivation_rules.why: Hardware-only barriers don't constrain the compiler — it can move accesses past the barrier in its IR. Compiler-only barriers don't constrain the hardware. C++/Rust atomics insert both; raw assembly barriers without compiler hints are bugs in C/C++.

derivation_rules.name: relaxed_atomics_for_counters_only
if: the only requirement is atomicity (not ordering)
then: relaxed atomic is sufficient and cheapest
derivation_rules.why: Counters incrementing in any order are fine — only the final count matters. Relaxed atomic gives atomicity with zero extra ordering cost. Misuse (relaxed for synchronisation) is a common bug.
